title: Requirements
body: Requirements What you need before installing. To put it together, go to Fast installation . What you need Computer Raspberry Pi 4 (this is what the rig was built and measured on) Surface Native Instruments Maschine MK2, over USB Audio Nothing extra required. The Pi's own headphone output works, and every figure in this project was measured on it at 48 kHz. An external interface Zynthian supports is optional and will sound better — but it is not what any of this was tested against Storage SD card, 16 GB or more — the ZynthianOS image is about 7.5 GB compressed Display Any HDMI monitor or TV for Zynthian's own UI, driven with a USB mouse and keyboard. A touchscreen is what the instrument was built around and is far nicer to play, but it is not required to install . You do need a screen eventually: saving snapshots happens there and nowhere else Network The Pi must reach the internet during installation

title: Fast installation
body: Fast installation Check the system requirements first — the hardware and the SD card matter, and nothing below works without them. Recommended. Six actions. About forty minutes, most of it unattended. At the end the instrument is running the factory snapshot: eight channels alive, the Maschine's pads lit in channel colours, both displays showing their tab rows, and a pattern playing the moment you press Play. Every step here is done by hand and explained in Manual installation . Come back to that page if something goes wrong, or if you would rather not run a script you have not read. 1 — Flash ZynthianOS Download the image and its checksum, verify it, then write it to the card with Raspberry Pi Imager. A truncated download produces a Pi that boots most of the way and then behaves inexplicably. curl -O https://os.zynthian.org/2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz curl -O https://os.zynthian.org/2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz.md5 md5sum -c 2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz.md5 # → 2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz: OK Use this exact build. Newer vangelis images are a different, still-beta release train and nothing here has been tested on them. Give Raspberry Pi Imager the compressed file exactly as it downloaded. Do not unpack it first — Imager reads .img.xz as it is. In Imager choose Use custom , pick the file, pick the card, write. Zynthian's own walkthrough is Get the firmware . 2 — Boot the Pi The first boot is an initialisation pass, not a normal boot. Give it about half an hour and do not cut the power. ZynthianOS resizes its filesystem and configures itself the first time it comes up, and the touchscreen does not work reliably while that runs — a blank, frozen or garbled screen here is the install working, not a dead Pi. Everything below depends on this finishing, so let it finish. Upstream describes it as First Boot . Budget for the whole job: flashing and first boot about 30 minutes , the installer in step 5 about 10 minutes , so 40 minutes end to end, nearly all of it waiting. Card in, network cable in, power on. A display is optional — see below. ZynthianOS resizes its filesystem and starts its own UI. 3 — Find it on the network The install runs over SSH, so the Pi has to be reachable first. A cable straight from the Pi to your computer is enough; so is a switch. Boot the first time with a cable, or with a display. A fresh card holds no WiFi credentials and cannot be given any over WiFi — the admin menu needs a screen, webconf needs a network. Set the WiFi up once by either route, and the Pi is headless and cordless from then on. You have How to reach it A display The UI comes up on HDMI. Admin → Network Info shows the address No display Reach it by name: zynthian.local , or zynthian.lan . http://zynthian.local in a browser is webconf; ssh root@zynthian.local needs no address at all If neither name resolves, your machine is not doing mDNS — WSL2 never does. Take the Pi's address off your router; every URL and command here accepts it in place of the name. What Login webconf, in a browser password opensynth SSH user root , password opensynth — older images use raspberry Factory defaults, the same on every Zynthian. Change them in webconf before the instrument sits on a network you do not control. This is the step that traps newcomers — everything after it assumes the Pi answers. If it does not, Reaching the Pi in section 4 works through it at length: both ways out of the WiFi deadlock, the switch and direct-cable wiring, and what to do when the names do not resolve. Upstream's own tutorials are No Hardware Build and Accessing Zynthian from your computer . 4 — Log in over SSH ssh root@192.168.2.123 # substitute your own address # or, if the name resolves: ssh root@zynthian.local # password: opensynth # older images: raspberry As root , not as a user with sudo . That is how ZynthianOS is administered — the installer checks, and refuses to run as anyone else. 5 — Run one command curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Witzman/Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII/main/bootstrap.sh | bash This takes about ten minutes and looks like it has hung. It compiles the HID daemon on the Pi. Do not interrupt it. It ends by loading the factory snapshot and restarting Zynthian's UI, so the instrument is playing-ready when it returns. 6 — Press Play The snapshot is already loaded. The installer places it as Zynthian's default snapshot and restarts the UI, so the instrument comes up by itself on a fresh Pi. Nothing to tap. You should see this: Where What Touchscreen mixer eight strips plus main MK2 left display tab row A KICK , B SNAR , C CLAP , D CHAT MK2 right display tab row E OHAT , F BASS , G LEAD , H PADS MK2 Group buttons lit in channel colours MK2 mode buttons exactly one lit — CONTROL Nothing happened? What you see What it means What to do Pads dark, displays blank The daemon is not running systemctl status maschine-mk2 , then restart the daemon first and the UI second — the order matters Pads lit, but nothing responds The driver never bound to the daemon's port Re-run the installer; it re-applies the zynautoconnect patch A tab is dashed That channel is silent on purpose — muted, or its generator is set to never fire Not a fault. The dashed tab is the instrument's way of explaining silence Zynthian came up empty, no mixer strips This Pi had a previous session. Zynthian restores its last state before falling back to the factory default Load it by hand: Snapshots → into bank 000 → 017-generative-techno . From the screen, or from webconf's Snapshots page Anything else: work through Manual installation , which gives each step's own check.

title: Features
body: Features An eight-channel generative groovebox on Zynthian, played entirely from a Native Instruments Maschine MK2 — pads, encoders, both displays, LEDs. Five euclidean drum channels and three Turing-machine voices, all eight always alive; nothing is created or torn down while playing. The generator owns the pattern. You do not draw a beat. You set hits, rotation and randomness, and the driver writes real notes into Zynthian's own sequencer — so patterns persist in snapshots and the touchscreen pattern editor mirrors exactly what the pads show. How to play it starts at Quick start ; how it is built is Internals . The eight channels Group Name Kind Engine MIDI ch Colour A KICK drum LinuxSampler, an SFZ drum machine 1 red B SNAR drum LinuxSampler 2 orange C CLAP drum LinuxSampler 3 amber D CHAT drum LinuxSampler 4 yellow-green E OHAT drum LinuxSampler 5 green F BASS voice JC303 6 blue G LEAD voice Obxd 7 violet H PADS voice padthv1 8 cyan Drums are warm colours and voices cool, so the seam between the halves is visible on the panel without reading anything. All eight are always alive — nothing is created or torn down while playing. The factory snapshot ships one channel against that grain. E · OHAT keeps its Simmons kit and its sampler, but arrives switched to voice behaviour: the Turing register walks the kit's own samples rather than euclid placing them. It is there so the switch below is audible the moment you plug in. Its tab reads VOX , and GRID blinks while it is selected. What it does Each of these has a page with a walkthrough on the real instrument. Generating patterns Euclidean drums and Turing-machine voices. You set hits, rotation and randomness; the generator writes the notes and you steer it. Playing and recording The pads are the instrument. Hold REC and what you play is captured into the same pattern the generator writes — and the pattern becomes yours. Modulation Hold MOD and every encoder stops setting a value and starts setting how that value moves. Saved with the set, still running tomorrow. Sound and presets Kits, samples and engine presets, changed while the rig plays — and switching what a channel behaves as without swapping its engine. Deep parameter control Eight knobs reaching a synth's fortieth parameter, on pages built from whatever the plugin publishes. Mixing and effects One control across all eight channels, two post-fader inserts on every one, and the globals that belong to the machine. The surface Every button, both displays, what each light means, and the list to work down when a channel goes quiet. Saving your work What a snapshot carries, what it cannot, and the one control in the web interface that looks like a save button and is not. What it is not No song mode, no pattern chaining, no sampling, no audio recording. Eight channels, always alive. It is an instrument for playing a single evolving pattern, not a workstation for arranging one.

title: Quick start
body: Quick start Two minutes from a running rig to something worth listening to. Everything here is reversible and nothing needs saving to keep playing. Your first two minutes Press Play . All eight channels start together, and the factory snapshot already holds a beat and three voices. Press Group A to select KICK, then STEP . Encoder 1 is HITS: turn it to 4 and you have four-on-the-floor. Encoder 2 is ROTATE — turn it and the same four hits slide around the bar without changing how many there are. Press Group F for BASS, still in STEP. Encoder 3 is MELODY. Turn it to roughly 30 and the bassline starts mutating a note at a time. When a phrase goes past that you want, turn MELODY back to 0: the cell reads LOCK and that line is now frozen, bit for bit, until you move the knob again. Press CONTROL and the same eight encoders become what the channel sounds like instead of what it plays. That is the whole instrument in miniature — a mode decides what the knobs mean, the channel decides what they act on. Nothing you have touched is destructive, and nothing needs saving to keep playing. When you do want to keep it, see Saving a set . Where next Every feature has a page with a walkthrough like the one above — the full list is on Features . The three worth reading first: Generating patterns — euclid, the Turing register, and what LOCK really means Modulation — making any sound parameter move on its own The surface — every button, and what to check when a channel goes quiet

body: Manual installation This is what bootstrap.sh does, step by step, for readers installing by hand or debugging an install that went wrong. Every step states what it does, why it is needed, and how to confirm it worked. This page starts from a Pi that already runs ZynthianOS. Flashing the card is not part of the install — it happens before any of it, and it is the same for both routes: step 1 of Fast installation has the image, the checksum and how to write it, and Zynthian's own walkthrough is Get the firmware . The first boot is an initialisation pass, not a normal boot. Give it about half an hour and do not cut the power. ZynthianOS resizes its filesystem and configures itself the first time it comes up, and the touchscreen does not work reliably while that runs — a blank, frozen or garbled screen here is the install working, not a dead Pi. Nothing below can be reached until it finishes. Upstream describes it as First Boot . Run everything on the Pi, as root , from the repository root. ZynthianOS is administered as root, and root SSH login is enabled out of the box. There is also a zynthian user in the sudo group, but nothing here uses it — bootstrap.sh refuses to run below uid 0, and the steps below assume root: ssh root@zynthian.local # or the IP; password: opensynth, older images raspberry git clone https://github.com/Witzman/Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII cd Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII Reaching the Pi Everything below is typed on the Pi over SSH, so start by getting there. An ethernet cable straight from the Pi to your computer works, and so does a switch. Plan on a cable or a display for the first contact — WiFi cannot be set up over WiFi. A freshly flashed card holds no WiFi credentials, and every way of giving it some needs the Pi already reachable: the admin menu needs a screen, webconf and VNC need a network. Boot a fresh card with no cable and it joins nothing, with no way in. The hotspot has the same catch — it is switched on from the admin menu, so it is a convenience once you are in, not a way of getting in. Way out of it What you do Display, once Attach HDMI, set the WiFi up in the UI's admin menu, unplug the display. It never needs to come back Cable, once Boot with ethernet, take the address, reach webconf or VNC, set the WiFi up there, unplug the cable Either one is a one-off. After it the Pi comes up on WiFi by itself and the rig is headless for good. Route How Display attached The UI comes up on HDMI. Admin → Network Info shows the address. It also appears on the error screen No display ssh root@zynthian.local , or http://zynthian.local for webconf. zynthian.lan is the same machine under a second name Neither name resolves Your side is not doing mDNS. Some systems need it enabled; WSL2 never resolves .local . Take the address from your router and use it in place of the name What Login webconf password opensynth SSH user root , password opensynth . Older images use raspberry These are factory defaults, identical on every Zynthian. Change them in webconf before the instrument sits on a network you do not control. None of this is ours — it is stock Zynthian, and the project's own wiki is the place to go when a route here does not fit your setup. No Hardware Build covers flashing, first boot and the network from scratch; Accessing Zynthian from your computer is the fuller list of ways in — VNC, SFTP, WiFi hotspot, and the Windows and macOS notes. Before you start Confirm the machine is what the rest of this page assumes. Check Command Expected OS build head -1 /zynthian/build_info.txt contains Oram-2601-1 UI branch git -C /zynthian/zynthian-ui branch --show-current oram-2601.1 webconf open http://<pi> the configuration page loads A different branch means another release train. Nothing here has been run on vangelis , which is still beta. The daemon and the driver Step 1 — Build the daemon What. Compiles the Rust HID daemon that speaks to the Maschine. Why. No binary is shipped; the daemon is built where it runs. How to confirm. daemon/target/release/maschine exists and is executable. apt install -y rustc cargo cd daemon && cargo build --release && cp picturetest.png target/release/ && cd .. Minutes on a Pi 4. Do not interrupt it. Step 2 — Put the daemon config in place What. Installs pad note offsets, encoder CC numbers, and external_pad_leds . Why. Without "external_pad_leds": true the daemon repaints the pads itself in its own global colour, and the first pad you touch destroys the driver's per-channel picture. How to confirm. The grep prints the flag as true . cp system/maschine.json daemon/maschine.json grep external_pad_leds daemon/maschine.json # → "external_pad_leds": true Step 3 — Install the udev rule What. Creates the stable /dev/maschine symlink and restarts the daemon on replug. Why. Otherwise the daemon must be pointed at a /dev/hidrawN number that moves between boots. How to confirm. /dev/maschine exists and points at a hidraw node. install -m 0644 system/99-maschine.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/99-maschine.rules udevadm control --reload-rules udevadm trigger --subsystem-match=hidraw Step 4 — Install the helper scripts What. Puts the JACK connect and clock helpers in /usr/local/bin . Why. maschine-jack-connect.sh sets the port alias virtual:maschine.rs/Maschine MK2 Pads . Zynthian derives a control-device id from the part of an alias after the first / , and a2j gives user-client ports no alias at all — without it the driver has no id to bind to and never loads. How to confirm. All three files are present and executable. install -m 0755 system/maschine-jack-connect.sh /usr/local/bin/ install -m 0755 system/maschine-clock-bridge.py /usr/local/bin/ install -m 0755 system/maschine-clock-connect.sh /usr/local/bin/ Step 5 — Install and enable the systemd units What. Installs the daemon, its web editor and the clock bridge as services. Why. The daemon must survive reboots and reconnect to JACK by itself. How to confirm. systemctl is-active maschine-mk2 prints active , and the MK2's displays light. install -m 0644 system/maschine-mk2.service /etc/systemd/system/ install -m 0644 system/maschine-web.service /etc/systemd/system/ install -m 0644 system/maschine-clock.service /etc/systemd/system/ systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable --now maschine-mk2 maschine-web maschine-clock If you cloned anywhere other than /root/Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII , edit ExecStart and WorkingDirectory in maschine-mk2.service , and --directory in maschine-web.service . install.sh rewrites these for you; by hand it is on you. Step 6 — Let a2jmidid export software clients What. Makes the daemon's ALSA sequencer port visible in JACK. Why. Without a JACK port, step 4's script has nothing to connect or alias. How to confirm. The port appears. jack_lsp | grep "Pads MIDI" # → a2j:maschine rs [N] (playback): Maschine MK2 Pads MIDI Step 7 — Patch zynautoconnect What. The only change to a Zynthian core file: adds the Pads port to the hardware-MIDI-source whitelist so it gets a zmip slot, and pins the stable uid. Why. Without it the driver never binds and the rig does nothing, with no error in any log — the most confusing failure in this project. Internally Zynthian gets as far as Found and never reaches Loaded , but both are INFO messages you will not see at the default log level; see step 10. How to confirm. The grep returns 1 or more. python3 tools/patch-autoconnect-maschine.py grep -c "maschine rs.*Pads MIDI" /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zynautoconnect/zynthian_autoconnect.py It ships as a patcher rather than a copy, so it edits your file. It is idempotent. Re-run it after every Zynthian system update — an update replaces zynthian_autoconnect.py and takes the binding with it. Step 8 — Copy the three driver files What. Drops the control-surface driver into Zynthian's ctrldev directory. Why. Two traps. These are untracked drop-ins in a checkout that tracks upstream, so never use git in /zynthian/zynthian-ui — a git reset --hard deletes them and the running instrument with them. And every module there needs a dev_ids attribute; without it the whole UI crash-loops every 14 seconds. How to confirm. All three files are present in the target directory. install -m 0644 ctrldev/zynthian_ctrldev_maschine_mk2.py \ ctrldev/techno_lib.py \ ctrldev/maschine_mk2_lib.py \ /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngine/ctrldev/ Step 9 — Restart, daemon first and UI second What. Brings both halves up in the one order that works. Why. Restarting the daemon alone makes a2j re-register the Pads port onto a new zmip slot while the driver stays bound to the dead one. The rig goes silent, no error appears anywhere, and a stale route is left behind that makes every later pad tap fire twice. How to confirm. Zynthian's UI comes back on the display. systemctl restart maschine-mk2 sleep 8 systemctl restart zynthian Step 10 — Confirm the surface is alive What. Proves the driver bound and the routing is clean. Why. No route means step 7 did not take effect; two routes mean a stale one from an earlier session is still alive, and every pad tap will fire twice. How to confirm. Exactly one ZynMidiRouter:devN_in under the Pads port. jack_lsp -c | awk '/\(capture\): Pads MIDI/{f=1;next} /^[^ \t]/{f=0} f{print}' # → ZynMidiRouter:dev2_in ← exactly one line, and nothing else Do not expect a particular slot number. Patched Zynthian assigns the slot itself, and it varies; this rig runs on dev2_in . Nothing else may connect that port — a second connector is what produced a duplicate route here, and two routes make every pad tap fire twice. See Why there is no "Loaded" line below before hunting through the journal. Why not grep -A3 . The obvious form of this check, jack_lsp -c | grep -A3 "Pads MIDI" , reports a healthy rig as a broken one. It matches the Pads port twice — once as a port and once as another port's connection — and the three lines it then prints are unrelated ports sitting at the left margin: a2j:maschine rs [129] (capture): Pads MIDI ZynMidiRouter:dev2_in ← the only real route a2j:maschine rs [129] (playback): MIDI Control ttymidi:MIDI_in -- a2j:maschine rs [129] (capture): Pads MIDI ZynMidiRouter:dev3_in ← these three are ports, not routes ZynMidiRouter:dev4_in ZynMidiRouter:dev5_in Four devN_in lines, one actual route. Read that as a fault and the fix you would reach for — disconnecting the "extras" — breaks a rig that was working. Indentation is the whole distinction: a route is indented under its port, a port starts at the left margin. The awk form above prints only the indented lines belonging to the Pads capture port, so it cannot mislead. With no snapshot loaded the MK2 draws both tab rows, the Group buttons in channel colours, and the CONTROL button lit. Nothing sounds yet — no chains exist. Plugins and drum kits Step 11 — Install the packaged plugins What. Installs three of the five engines from Debian. Why. obxd-lv2 is channel G, padthv1-lv2 is channel H, and tap-lv2 provides TAP Reverberator and TAP Stereo Echo for all sixteen inserts. How to confirm. Three Status: install ok installed lines. apt install -y obxd-lv2 padthv1-lv2 tap-lv2 dpkg -s obxd-lv2 padthv1-lv2 tap-lv2 | grep ^Status Step 12 — Confirm JC303 What. Checks the bass engine, which is not a Debian package. Why. It comes from Zynthian's own plugin set; if missing, install it through webconf so the plugin cache learns about it. How to confirm. The directory exists. ls -d /zynthian/zynthian-plugins/lv2/JC303.lv2 Step 13 — Enable the plugins and regenerate the LV2 cache What. In webconf: Engines , enable Obxd, padthv1, JC303, TAP Reverberator and TAP Stereo Echo, then Regenerate LV2 Cache . Why. A plugin that is installed but not enabled is invisible to a snapshot, and loading one that names a disabled plugin gives a chain with no engine. How to confirm. All five appear as available engines. Let the scan finish before loading anything. Step 14 — Confirm the SFZ drum kits What. Checks the kits the five drum channels play. Why. Missing kits load silently — the channels exist and make no sound. Use find -type f : one entry is a directory , so ls over-counts. How to confirm. A count greater than zero. find "/zynthian/zynthian-data/soundfonts/sfz/Drum Machines" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.sfz' | wc -l # → 40 (on the rig this was written from) The snapshot Step 15 — Copy it into a bank What. Places the factory snapshot in bank 000 . Why. The bank subdirectory is not optional — a snapshot at the snapshots root is invisible in the UI. How to confirm. The file is listed under 000/ . install -m 0644 snapshot/017-generative-techno.zss \ /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/000/ Step 16 — Make it the default, so it loads by itself What. Copies the same file to the snapshots root as default.zss . Why. At startup Zynthian restores last_state.zss if there is one, and otherwise falls back to default.zss — which is exactly the fresh-install case, so the instrument comes up without anyone touching a screen. default.zss is only ever written by an explicit save as default , so seeding it destroys nothing, and a Pi with an existing session keeps its own. How to confirm. Restart the UI; it comes up in the mixer, not the main menu. install -m 0644 snapshot/017-generative-techno.zss \ /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/default.zss systemctl restart zynthian Step 17 — Or load it by hand What. Opens Snapshots, goes into bank 000 , taps 017-generative-techno . Why. Needed only if this Pi already had a session, whose last_state.zss takes priority over the default. Loading takes about fifteen seconds: eight engines start, sixteen plugin hosts come up, and the driver re-reads its parameters out of the sequencer. How to confirm. Eight mixer strips plus main, both tab rows drawn. Never save from webconf's Snapshots page. Its Name: field plus the checkmark renames the selected bank — it has destroyed bank 000 here once. Loading from webconf is safe; saving from it is not. Step 18 — The genre pack What. Places fifty more snapshots, 031 – 080 , in the same bank. Why. They are fixed arrangements to start from — ten each of house, deep house, minimal, dub and trance — and unlike the factory snapshot they are optional : the instrument is complete without them. They are not copied over default.zss , because the factory snapshot is what a fresh Pi should boot into. How to confirm. Fifty files listed under 000/ . install -m 0644 snapshot/genre-pack/*.zss \ /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/000/ find /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/000 -name '0[3-8][0-9]-*.zss' | wc -l # → 50 bootstrap.sh does this for you; this step is for a hand install. Every voice in the pack arrives at LOCK with no modulation, so a preset plays the same bar until you turn something. Notes You do not need a touchscreen The UI is ordinary HDMI: a monitor or TV with a USB mouse and keyboard drives it, and webconf's Snapshots page loads a snapshot from a browser with no screen attached at all. A touchscreen is what the instrument was built around and is far nicer to play — but the rig runs headless, and only saving a snapshot needs the UI itself. Which does not have to be a physical screen. Zynthian ships a VNC server — webconf, INTERFACE → UI Options → Enable VNC Server — and the whole UI then runs in a browser at http://zynthian.local:6080/vnc.html , with the engines' own desktop on :6081 . Confirmed working on this rig. That is the headless answer for anything the UI owns, snapshot saving included: a Pi with no display, no keyboard and no mouse is still fully driveable from the computer you installed from. Why there is no "Loaded" line Zynthian logs Found ctrldev driver … and Loaded ctrldev driver … at INFO , while ZYNTHIAN_LOG_LEVEL defaults to WARNING (30). On a stock rig neither line is ever written, whether the driver loaded or not, so their absence proves nothing — the JACK route in step 10 is the check that works as shipped. To see them, uncomment the line Zynthian ships for it in /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zynthian.sh , set it to 20, and restart the UI: export ZYNTHIAN_LOG_LEVEL=20 # 10=DEBUG, 20=INFO, 30=WARNING (the default) systemctl restart zynthian Measured, not assumed: at level 20 the two lines appear as INFO:zynthian_ctrldev_manager.update_available_drivers: Found ctrldev driver 'zynthian_ctrldev_maschine_mk2' for devices with ID 'Maschine MK2 Pads' INFO:zynthian_ctrldev_manager.load_driver: Loaded ctrldev driver 'Maschine MK2 Drum Rig' for 'Maschine MK2 Pads'. Note what the Loaded line is keyed on. It carries the driver's display name, Maschine MK2 Drum Rig — not the module name. A grep for maschine_mk2 finds the Found line and misses the Loaded one, which is the one that matters. Grep for ctrldev driver instead. zynthian.sh is a core Zynthian file, so a system update reverts it. There is no setting for this in webconf. Verify bash tools/check-prereqs.sh; echo "exit=$?" # → exit=0 once loaded jack_lsp | grep -c TAP # → 64 cd ctrldev && python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -q # → Ran 271 tests … OK The unit tests run anywhere — no Pi, no Maschine. They are the only automated proof this project has: the driver cannot be imported off the Pi, so everything generative and presentational lives in techno_lib.py , which has no Zynthian imports and is tested. When it does not work Symptom Cause Fix Displays blank, buttons dark, Zynthian fine daemon not running systemctl status maschine-mk2 , then journalctl -u maschine-mk2 -n 50 Surface dead, no devN_in under the Pads port no zmip slot — the driver never bound Step 7, then restart daemon and UI No Pads MIDI in jack_lsp a2jmidid not exporting software clients Step 6 Every pad tap fires twice a stale JACK route Step 10, using the awk form — only an indented second devN_in is a real duplicate. Repair by restarting the daemon, then the UI Whole UI restarts every ~14 s a module in ctrldev/ without dev_ids Step 8 First pad touch destroys the pad colours external_pad_leds missing Step 2, then restart the daemon and the UI Input dies after seconds, then recovers kernel hidraw fault; the daemon reopens the device Nothing to do. watchdog: input stalled, reopened about every 8 s is healthy A channel is silent, tab dashed muted, or its generator is silent — HITS 0, or play chance 0 Not a fault. Raise HITS or CHANCE, or unmute with its F button A channel is silent, tab normal engines did not start jack_lsp | grep -c TAP → 64. Fewer means plugin instances failed Every channel silent something is soloed Tap SOLO to leave solo mode

title: Internals

headings.text: Why zynautoconnect has to be patched
The insert pair, measured on the wire
Sixteen inserts without placing sixteen processors

body: Internals How the instrument is built. What it does is Features ; how to install it is Manual installation . The control path A pad press reaches the sequencer through five hops, and every one of them has broken at least once: flowchart LR HID["Maschine MK2 USB HID"] --> D["maschine daemon Rust"] D --> A["a2jmidid virtual port"] A --> Z["ZynMidiRouter zmip slot"] Z --> C["ctrldev driver Python"] C --> S["zynseq Zynthian's sequencer"] The daemon owns the hardware: it reads HID reports, drives both 255×64 displays and the LEDs, and exposes an ALSA sequencer port. a2jmidid lifts that port into JACK. Zynthian then has to be persuaded to treat it as a hardware MIDI source so it is given a zmip slot — and that is the patch below. Encoders are relative. The daemon holds each encoder's value as device state and moves it by the hardware delta. Real movement is 0-4 units per report and a counter wrap reads as −38 to −40, so the wrap guard is 8. The big encoder sends 8 units per detent and wraps 120 → 0, sitting exactly on that threshold, so it needs its own delta path. Why zynautoconnect has to be patched It is the only Zynthian core file this project changes, and it ships as an idempotent patcher rather than a copy, so it edits your version instead of overwriting it. Two changes. The Pads port joins the list of ports treated as hardware MIDI sources, which is what earns it a zmip slot. And the uid virtual:maschine.rs/Maschine MK2 Pads is pinned, because the ALSA client number embedded in the port name changes across boots while a ctrldev driver binds by device id. Unpatched, the driver never binds: Zynthian gets as far as Found and never reaches Loaded . The rig does nothing, and no log anywhere says why — literally, because both of those messages are logged at INFO while ZYNTHIAN_LOG_LEVEL defaults to WARNING, so neither is written on a stock rig. The check that works is the JACK route: exactly one ZynMidiRouter:devN_in under the Pads port. Re-run the patcher after every Zynthian update: an update replaces the file and takes the binding with it. The driver The generator owns the pattern. The driver does not synthesise notes at play time — it writes them into zynseq, which is why patterns survive in snapshots and why the touchscreen editor shows the same thing the pads do. Playing is Zynthian's job; the driver only decides what is written. Three facts hold the design together. Everything testable lives outside the driver. The driver itself cannot be imported off the Pi — it needs zynlibs.zynseq — so the Turing register and its mutation, the undo ring, register-to-pitch quantisation, euclidean placement, the gate mask, and the whole page and column model were pushed into techno_lib.py , which has no Zynthian imports. That module carries its own test suite, including the invariant the instrument rests on: a generator at LOCK produces a byte-identical register over 500 iterations — which now has to hold for the rhythm register as well as the pitch one. Every zynseq call holds one lock. libzynseq is not thread-safe and the driver reaches it from three threads — the MIDI handler, a queued signal handler and a 30 Hz playhead poll. Without the lock the entire Zynthian UI died with a segfault about 95 seconds into a jam. Nothing slow runs on the MIDI thread. Loading a preset blocks on a socket for seconds while the MIDI handler holds the lock for the whole event, so preset and kit changes are deferred to the poll thread. A silent channel must say why. Play chance 0 emits nothing and looked exactly like a hang, so a channel that cannot sound draws its tab dashed. It is the one mechanism the surface has for explaining silence. The factory snapshot The eight chains Chain Title in the snapshot Engine MIDI channel (0-based in the file) A Kick LS/LinuxSampler 0 B Snare LS/LinuxSampler 1 C Clap LS/LinuxSampler 2 D Closed Hat LS/LinuxSampler 3 E Open Hat LS/LinuxSampler 4 F BASS JV/JC303 5 G LEAD JV/Obxd 6 H PADS JV/padthv1 7 The MIDI channel is the contract , not the title and not the order — the driver resolves a channel to a chain by MIDI channel, so titles are free and numbers are not. All five drum chains share one LinuxSampler process, so eight SFZ kits cost about 250 MB in total rather than per channel. The insert pair, measured on the wire zynmixer:output_NNa/b → TAP_Stereo_Echo-NN → TAP_Reverberator-NN → zynmixer:input_17 Echo first, reverb second, so the reverb hears the echo's repeats. The order was read out of jack_lsp -c on the running rig, not assumed. The inserts are fed from the strip's output , which is what makes them post-fader: they inherit the fader and the mute, so muting a channel takes its reverb and delay tail with it. Both plugins have a true wet level, not a dry/wet crossfade — sweep the wet to maximum and the dry is still there at the same level. That is what lets encoders 7 and 8 behave like sends. Every cheaper candidate measured turned out to be a crossfade. Four ports are forced rather than left at their defaults: Plugin Port Value Why TAP Stereo Echo dryLevel 0.0 dB Ships at −4 dB; across the pair that quietly costs every channel about 8 dB TAP Stereo Echo lecholevel , recholevel −70.0 dB Wet starts closed; encoder 8 opens it TAP Reverberator drylevel 0.0 dB Same reason TAP Reverberator wetlevel −70.0 dB Wet starts closed; encoder 7 opens it Gain staging Channel strips 0.19 , main 0.80 . That is measurement, not caution: one sampler channel peaks at 1.24 before the mixer, and eight summed to 2.92 on the main bus — nearly three times full scale. The sampler's own volume is not the lever; taking it from 96 to 40 moved the bus peak by about 1.5 dB. Sixteen inserts without placing sixteen processors Build one channel by hand on the touchscreen — add TAP Stereo Echo, then TAP Reverberator, set the four values, save — and let tools/build-techno-snapshot.py replicate it. The cloner finds the chain carrying both inserts, appends the same two to every other chain that has a MIDI channel, gives each a fresh processor id, copies the template's fader position, and backs the file up first. Then load and save once more from the touchscreen, so what is on disk is Zynthian's own output rather than the script's. It deliberately does not build the whole snapshot. Nothing outside the UI process can reach Zynthian's live state manager, and hand-maintaining fader positions in JSON is exactly the kind of guess this project avoids. Back to: Requirements · Features

title: Touchscreen patch
body: Touchscreen patch Optional. Not part of the instrument. Apply it only if you have the symptom below. Who needs this Your touchscreen reports touches at the wrong place — usually compressed into one corner or scaled toward one edge — while the same screen displays correctly. That happens when the panel's touch controller reports coordinates in its own native resolution while Zynthian's UI is running at a different configured display size. Zynthian passes the raw touch value straight through, so a panel reporting 0-4095 on a 800×480 UI puts every touch in the top-left eighth of the screen. This was the case on the rig this guide was written from: an Elecrow 5" 800×480 panel, HDMI for video and USB for touch. If your touch already lands where you press, skip this page. The patch edits a Zynthian core file, and there is no reason to carry a change you do not need. The patch It scales the raw touch value onto Zynthian's configured display size, guarding against a zero maximum so an unreported range cannot divide by zero. File: /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py , in MultiTouch 's evdev event loop. @@ class MultiTouch(object): elif evdev_event.code == ecodes.ABS_MT_POSITION_X: - if self._invert_x: - self._current_touch.x_root = self.max_x - evdev_event.value - else: - self._current_touch.x_root = evdev_event.value + raw = self.max_x - evdev_event.value if self._invert_x else evdev_event.value + self._current_touch.x_root = int(raw * zynthian_gui_config.display_width / self.max_x) if self.max_x else raw if self._current_touch not in self.events: self.events.append(self._current_touch) elif evdev_event.code == ecodes.ABS_MT_POSITION_Y: - if self._invert_y: - self._current_touch.y_root = self.max_y - evdev_event.value - else: - self._current_touch.y_root = evdev_event.value + raw = self.max_y - evdev_event.value if self._invert_y else evdev_event.value + self._current_touch.y_root = int(raw * zynthian_gui_config.display_height / self.max_y) if self.max_y else raw if self._current_touch not in self.events: self.events.append(self._current_touch) Both hunks keep the existing _invert_x / _invert_y handling and only add the scaling on top of it. Applying it Back the file up first — this is a Zynthian core file, not one of ours. ssh root@<pi> cp /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py \ /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py.bak # edit the two handlers as shown above systemctl restart zynthian Verify: press each corner of the screen and confirm the UI responds at that corner. To undo it: cp /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py.bak \ /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py systemctl restart zynthian Two warnings A Zynthian update overwrites it. multitouch.py is tracked in the zynthian-ui checkout, so any update replaces your edit. Keep the .bak , and expect to re-apply after upgrading. Do not run git checkout or git reset in /zynthian/zynthian-ui to undo this. That directory also holds this project's three driver files as untracked drop-ins; a hard reset removes the instrument along with the patch. Restore from the .bak copy instead. Back to: Requirements · Manual installation

title: Deep parameter control
body: Deep parameter control Eight knobs, and a synth with forty parameters. This is how you reach the fortieth without a menu. What it is Page 1 of CONTROL gives a voice the four controls anyone reaches for first — CUTOFF, RESO, ENV, DECAY. Everything else the plugin publishes fills further CONTROL pages , eight ports to a page, in the plugin's own order and under the plugin's own names. Nothing in the driver knows what those parameters are. It asks the plugin what it has and builds the pages from the answer, which is why a synth nobody planned for still works. Try it Select Group G (LEAD) and press CONTROL . That is page 1 — PRESET, CUTOFF, RESO, ENV, DECAY, LEVEL, REVERB, DELAY. Press the right arrow beside the display. Page 2. The names change to the plugin's own — abbreviated to fit, in the order the plugin lists them. Keep pressing. Each page is eight more ports. A large synth runs to several pages. Turn any of them. Each port is driven as a percentage of its own range, so a knob behaves the same whether the port runs 0–1 or 0–20000. Hold TEMPO and turn the same knob. Twice as fast. Hold it to get near, let go to land. Press CONTROL again to jump straight back to page 1 rather than paging around. How it works The four synth knobs follow the plugin that is loaded , not the one the snapshot shipped with. Change a chain's engine from the touchscreen and CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY rebind to the new plugin's own ports. Host plumbing is filtered out. Plugins publish ports no player can use — freewheel flags, latency reports, enable switches that are not really switches. Those are recognised and dropped, so a generated page is eight things you might actually turn. Discreteness is respected. A port with a handful of positions steps in whole units; a continuous one moves by percentage with the remainder carried, so slow turns still move it. TEMPO changes how far a turn goes, never what it sets. A speed, not a mode: nothing latches, and the same knob reaches the same values either way. It applies to every encoder on the instrument, not only these. What it refuses, and why A role the plugin has no port for draws dead. If a loaded synth publishes no resonance, the RESO column greys out and its encoder does nothing at all. That is the same law the whole surface follows: a knob with no source is drawn dead rather than showing a number it cannot move. A knob that silently does nothing is the worst object on a control surface, because you cannot tell it apart from a broken one. See also Sound and presets — page 1, and changing the engine underneath it Modulation — every generated port can carry a modulator

title: Generating patterns
body: Generating patterns You do not draw a beat. You set hits, rotation and randomness, and the generator writes the notes. This is the machine's centre — everything else colours what happens here. What it is The driver writes real notes into Zynthian's own sequencer . Not a private buffer: because they are real notes in the real sequencer, patterns persist in snapshots and the touchscreen pattern editor mirrors exactly what the pads show. There are two generators, and every channel runs one of them: Euclidean , on the five drum channels. Given a step count and a hit count, hits spread as evenly as the grid allows, then rotate. Two Turing machines , on each of the three voices. One shift register is read as pitch, the other as which steps sound. Each is clocked once per pass and mutated by its own knob — MELODY and RHYTHM — so a melody can evolve over a rhythm that stays exactly where you put it. Which generator a channel runs is not fixed to its engine — see Sound and presets . Try it The drums. Press Play , then Group A to select KICK, then STEP . Turn encoder 1 (HITS) to 4. That is four-on-the-floor. Turn encoder 2 (ROTATE). The same four hits slide around the bar without changing how many there are. Turn HITS to 5. Five in sixteen is the clave. Try 3 in 8 for tresillo, or 7 in 16 for the busy one that still swings. The voices. Press Group F for BASS, still in STEP. Turn encoder 3 (MELODY) to about 30. The bassline starts fishing: every pass mutates one bit, so the line keeps turning into a neighbouring line. When a phrase goes past that you want, snap MELODY back to 0. The cell reads LOCK and that line is frozen, bit for bit, until you move the knob again. Missed it? Press NOTE REPEAT . It gives the previous line back and sets both knobs to 0 so it holds. Now put MELODY at LOCK and turn encoder 4 (RHYTHM) to about 30. The opposite: the notes hold still while steps appear and disappear underneath them. Both at LOCK, then tap pads in STEP mode. Each tap turns a step on or off, and it stays — tap step 1 and step 9, then turn MELODY up, and you have two notes evolving on the beat you chose. A KICK B SNAR C CLAP D CHAT HITS 0004 ROTATE 0000 DIVIDE 1/16 LENGTH 0016 The drum STEP page. HITS and ROTATE are the two you play with; DIVIDE and LENGTH set the frame. How it works The drum STEP page is HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE, LENGTH, VELO, CHANCE, SWING. HITS and ROTATE are the two you play with; the rest set the frame. CHANCE is how often a hit actually fires — drop it and the pattern starts breathing rather than repeating. The voice STEP page is DIVIDE, GATE, MELODY, RHYTHM, LENGTH, OCTAVE, RANGE, VELO. The two generators sit side by side because they are one idea. LENGTH here is the pitch register’s length in bits, not a bar count. GATE is how long each note holds — up to eight steps, so a pad can be a drone. The pitch value is quantised to ROOT and SCALE from the ALL page, then placed by OCTAVE and RANGE. MELODY is the instrument’s main gesture. Set it to 20–40 and the voice fishes. Snap it to 0 the moment you hear something worth keeping. The cell reads LOCK rather than a number, deliberately: a number could be a coincidence, while LOCK means nothing will rewrite that pattern at all. RHYTHM is the same gesture applied to the beat. Same range, same LOCK at zero, same freeze. Which steps sound is its own register, one bit per step, so it is independent of the notes: either can run while the other holds. A pad tap in STEP mode flips one of those bits, which is why a rhythm you tap in by hand survives everything — it is not an edit sitting on top of the generator, it is the generator. Structure lands on the bar; timbre lands instantly. A change to what the pattern is waits for the channel's own next wrap, so the groove never jumps under your hand. DIVIDE and LENGTH show in angle brackets — >1/8< — while a change is waiting to take. What it refuses, and why Pattern length is quantised to whole beats, and always will be. The sequencer stores a pattern as a number of beats, so the reachable step counts are whole beats times the steps in a beat. 1, 5, 7, 11 and 13 steps cannot be asked for. Turning LENGTH lands on the nearest count that exists rather than refusing to move — so if the number skips past where you aimed, that is the grid and not a fault. A silent channel says so. HITS at 0 is a silent channel, not a broken one, and CHANCE at 0 emits nothing at all. Both draw the channel's tab dashed — the instrument's one mechanism for explaining silence. Read the tab row before suspecting the rig. See also Modulation — how to make these values move on their own, and why the generator's own knobs refuse it Playing and recording — playing over the generator, and taking a pattern from it The surface — reading the tabs, and what to check when it goes quiet

title: Mixing and effects
body: Mixing and effects Balancing eight channels from eight knobs, the two effects every channel feeds, and the handful of settings that belong to the machine rather than to a channel. What it is Every channel carries its own reverb and delay send on encoders 7 and 8, feeding two shared effects. Sixteen insert hosts in total — a TAP Stereo Echo and a TAP Reverberator on every one of the eight channels. The sends are post-fader , so pulling a channel down takes its tail with it rather than leaving a ghost of it hanging in the reverb. Try it Press VOLUME. That is MIXER mode: one control across all eight channels at once, rather than eight controls on one channel. Turn any encoder. Each one is a channel's LEVEL. This is the page for balancing. Press the right arrow beside the display. The ring steps to REVERB, then DELAY — the same eight channels, a different send. Press VOLUME again to jump back to page 1 rather than paging round. Press AUTO. That is FILTER: CUTOFF and RESO across the row. Notice the five drum columns are drawn dead — see below. Press ALL. Now the eight encoders are the machine's globals: ROOT, SCALE, BPM, MASTER, REVSIZE, REVTYPE, DLYTIME, DLYFBK. How it works A spread page is one verb across eight channels. MIXER and FILTER are both spreads; CONTROL and STEP are the other shape, eight verbs on one channel. That is the whole grammar of the surface, and every page is one or the other. ROOT and SCALE wait for the bar , like everything else that changes what the pattern is. The rest of the globals land instantly. Group button brightness tracks each channel's level , so the row shows the balance without reading anything — and the peak meters on the display run live. What it refuses, and why FILTER's five drum columns draw dead. Only the three voices answer it. The drum channels run a sampler, and there is no filter in that chain to reach — so rather than offering a knob that would do nothing, the columns grey out. There is no drum filter in this version. That is worth saying plainly so you do not go hunting for one: filtering drums needs a filter plugin per channel, which costs eight more plugin hosts, and it has not been built. See also Modulation — a spread page is the best place to bind eight modulators at once Sound and presets — LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY per channel The surface — modes, pages and how the ring works

title: Modulation
body: Modulation Set how a value moves instead of what it is. Quick start gets you playing; this page is the second dimension underneath every knob you already know. What it is MOD is the SWING button. Hold it and every encoder stops setting a value and starts setting how that value moves . Tap it instead and it latches, so both hands are free. The button says which one you did: steady while you hold it, blinking while it is latched. Same blink GRID uses for an overridden kind, so the panel has one vocabulary and not two. It matters because a latched MOD outlives your finger — the encoders keep meaning depth and the refused columns keep their bars off until you tap it again. It is not a mode. It adds no page, no ring entry, and nothing to memorise: the map of parameters you already know does not change, and MOD gives every one of them a second dimension in the same place. It costs no plugin instances, and nothing is created or destroyed while you play. Try it Press Play and select a voice — Group G is LEAD. Press CONTROL. Encoder 2 is CUTOFF. Hold SWING — that is MOD — and turn encoder 2. The column's name gains a ~ and its bar grows a dashed span. You are setting how far the cutoff will travel, not where it sits. A small turn gives a narrow sweep; a bigger turn a broader one. Let go of SWING and listen. The filter sweeps on its own. Keep MOD held and tap pad 1 , then pad 12 . Pads 1–12 are the rates, slowest first: sixteen bars per cycle at one end, a sixteenth at the other. You should hear the sweep speed up dramatically between the two. Tap pads 13–16 for the four shapes — triangle, ramp, square, and sample-and-hold, which jumps to a new value each cycle and holds it there. Release MOD and turn encoder 2 again. Now you are steering the base — the centre the sweep moves around — and the sweep follows you there. Hold SWING and ERASE together and turn encoder 2. The modulation stops and the value returns to where you set it, not to wherever the sweep happened to stop. E OHAT F BASS G LEAD H PADS PRESET BA01 CUTOFF~ 0064 RESO 0032 ENV 0048 CUTOFF carries a modulator: the name gains a ~ , the bar shows the range it sweeps, and the value cell still reads the base — the number your hand owns. How it works Depth is bipolar, and centre is off. Turning back to the middle does not leave a dormant modulator behind — it removes it. The fastest way to stop something moving is to put its depth back where it started. Rates are locked to the bar , so a modulator lines up with the pattern it is colouring rather than drifting against it. Twelve rates and four shapes fill the sixteen pads exactly, with nothing unreachable. The value cell always shows the base. Motion lives on the indicator bar: a dashed span across the range the modulator covers, and a small tick travelling inside it. A fast modulator blurs into a static span, and that is honest — the span is the truth, the tick is a courtesy. On 1-bit glass refreshing five times a second, animating the number would just make it unreadable. On a spread page it is eight at once. Press VOLUME for the mixer, then MOD and each encoder in turn, and every channel gets its own modulator on the same control. They do not run in lockstep: each starts its cycle at the moment you bind it, so binding them one after another spreads them around the bar and the row breathes rather than pumps. It is saved. Modulators go into the snapshot with their depth, rate, shape and position, and the value stored is the base you set rather than wherever the sweep happened to be. Load the set tomorrow and they are still running, still spread apart. What it refuses, and why MOD will not bind to anything that rewrites the pattern. While MOD is down, those columns lose their bar — the name and the value stay, because they are still live controls; they just cannot be modulated. So the rule under MOD is simple: a bar means you can bind here . HITS · ROTATE · MELODY · RHYTHM · CHANCE · VELO · GATE · DIVIDE · LENGTH · KIT · PRESET · ROOT · SCALE The refusal is the design, not a gap. A modulator writes several times a second. A knob that rewrites the pattern would tear the line up continuously — and on a channel you had recorded onto, it would destroy your take with nothing on the surface explaining why. Nothing MOD can do will touch a recorded take. Generation moving on its own is a genuinely good idea and it is coming, but it needs its own answer to that question first. Clearing everything at once Hold MOD and ERASE and press ALL . Every modulator goes, and every value lands back where you put it. The markers vanish the instant you press it; the values themselves settle a moment later. That gap is deliberate — the instrument will not write twenty parameters inside a single button press, because doing that on the button thread once froze the whole machine. See also Features — everything the instrument does, in one list Quick start — your first two minutes

title: Playing and recording
body: Playing and recording The pads are the instrument. Hold REC while you play them and what you played is captured into the same pattern the generator writes — and from that moment the pattern is yours, not the machine's. What it is In CONTROL, ALL, MIXER and FILTER the sixteen pads play the selected channel. On a voice they are notes. On a drum every pad triggers that channel's own sound, because a drum channel is one sound — hearing CLAP while playing KICK would be the silent-channel confusion in a new costume. In STEP the pads are the step editor instead. A tap toggles that step, and the velocity of the tap becomes the step's velocity, so accents are played in rather than dialled. Step 0 is the top-left pad; the grid reads left to right, top to bottom. Try it Press Play , select Group F (BASS) and press CONTROL . Play the pads — that is the instrument. Hold REC and play a short phrase. Keep holding REC. Let go of the last pad while REC is still held , then release REC. Your phrase is in the pattern. Press STEP and look at the pads. The steps you played light amber ; the generated notes are still there underneath, dim or bright. Look at the page indicator. It reads PLAY — you own this pattern now, and the generator has stopped rewriting it. To give it back: hold ERASE and press Group F . Your take is gone and the generator resumes. That is deliberate and it is destructive. How it works Capture happens on release, not on press. A note's length is how long you held the pad, and that is not known until you let go. This has a consequence worth committing to memory: you must still be holding REC when you release the pad. Let go of REC first and the note sounds but is never captured. That is the same rule that lets you release REC without cutting off notes still ringing, so it is a trade rather than an oversight. Strikes quantise to the nearest step , wrapping at the end of the bar — nearest rather than next, so a strike landing a hair early is not pushed a step late. A note's length is clamped to what is left of the pattern. Recording adds; it does not overwrite. The generated line freezes where it is and your note goes on top, so a recorded step can hold two notes. An amber pad means your note is there and the generated one still is. A step that sounds but stays dark would be the defect. The page indicator reads REC while you are capturing , and REC-STOP if the transport is stopped — nothing is being captured then, and the surface says so rather than letting you play into nothing. Who owns the pattern The first captured note makes you the owner of that channel's pattern, and the generator stops rewriting it. The indicator reads PLAY for as long as that holds — including after a snapshot reload , because ownership is saved. Handing the pattern back is deliberate and destructive: your take is gone the moment it happens. There are two routes, and knowing which knobs do it is the difference between keeping a take and losing one. Route On a drum On a voice Gesture ERASE + the channel's Group button Knobs that hand back HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE LENGTH, DIVIDE, MELODY, RHYTHM Knobs that keep the take LENGTH, VELO, CHANCE, SWING GATE, OCTAVE, RANGE, VELO Two details worth carrying: a drum's LENGTH keeps the take, because shortening a pattern preserves the steps that still fit; and MELODY and RHYTHM only hand back when they move off LOCK , since a locked generator rewrites nothing and could not undo your recording anyway. A knob has to actually move — brushing one does nothing. On a drum channel the amber colouring does not survive a snapshot reload, and that is not a lost take. A played drum note carries the same pitch as a generated one, so once the pattern is read back there is nothing left to tell the two apart. The notes are all there and the channel is still yours: the indicator still reads PLAY , and after a reload that indicator, not the pad colour, is the authority. On a voice the amber survives, because the played pitch is its own. What it refuses, and why You cannot record in STEP mode — there the pads belong to the step editor — and you cannot record while MOD is active , where they pick a modulator's rate and shape. In both cases the REC button is unlit . A lit REC would be promising a take it cannot make, so it goes dark rather than letting you play a phrase into nothing and wonder why it vanished. See also Generating patterns — what you are playing over Modulation — why nothing MOD does can touch a recorded take The surface — the pad colours in full, and what to check when it goes quiet

title: Saving your work

headings.text: What it will not carry, and why

body: Saving your work A snapshot holds the whole instrument — patterns, sounds, levels, and the driver's own state. Two things it cannot hold, and one trap in the web interface. Try it On the touchscreen (or through VNC in a browser), open the snapshot list and enter a bank. The first entry is Save as new snapshot . That is the one. To load, pick any snapshot in the list. Everything comes back — including which channels you had switched, and who owned each pattern. The trap In webconf's Snapshots page, the Name field and its checkmark RENAME THE SELECTED BANK. They do not save a snapshot. It looks exactly like a save box. It is not one. Save from the touchscreen or VNC. What a snapshot carries The patterns themselves, play chance and swing, mixer levels and mutes, both effect sends per channel, and each channel's kit or preset. Plus the driver's own state, which exists nowhere else: every voice's Turing register and its four-deep undo ring, the voice parameters, the globals, which channels you switched kind on , who owns each pattern , your modulators — depth, rate, shape, position and base — and the mode and page you were in. A set saved mid-sweep comes back at the value you dialled in, not wherever a modulator happened to be when you saved. What it will not carry, and why A mute set on the sequencer does not persist. Mute the mixer strip instead — that is in the snapshot, and it shows on the touchscreen mixer too. Amber provenance on a drum channel does not survive a reload. Your take does; the colour does not. A played drum note has the same pitch as a generated one, so once the pattern is read back nothing can tell them apart. The PLAY indicator remains the authority. See also Playing and recording — what ownership means, and why amber matters Modulation — modulators are saved running

title: Sound and presets
body: Sound and presets What each channel sounds like, how to change it while the rig plays, and how to make a channel behave as something its engine is not. What it is CONTROL is the sound page, and it follows the engine. A drum engine gives you KIT and SAMPLE; a synth engine gives you PRESET, CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY. Encoders 6, 7 and 8 are LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY on every channel — the same three controls in the same place, always. The engine decides, not the behaviour. A sampler played by the Turing register still has a kit and a sample, so it still shows them. Switching a channel's kind changes how it is played, never what it is. Every channel keeps its engine for the life of the snapshot. Nothing is created or destroyed while you play, because building a plugin rebuilds the audio graph and that is a hole in the sound. Try it Select Group A (KICK) and press CONTROL . Encoder 1 is KIT, encoder 2 is SAMPLE. Turn SAMPLE. The kick changes to another sound inside the same kit, immediately. Press the button to the right of the big encoder. Same effect — it steps the selected channel's sound without using an encoder. Hold SHIFT and press it again. Now it steps the kit rather than the sample. Only a drum engine has kits, so on a synth channel this does nothing. Select Group G (LEAD) and press CONTROL . Now encoder 1 is PRESET and encoders 2–5 are CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY. Turn CUTOFF. You are driving the synth that is actually loaded, not a fixed idea of one. Now the interesting one. Select Group E (OHAT) and hold SHIFT while pressing GRID . The channel changes what it behaves as. Do it again to change back. One channel arrives switched E · OHAT ships as a voice. It keeps its Simmons kit and its sampler, but the Turing register drives it rather than euclid, so it walks between samples instead of laying down a straight hat. If your open hat wanders and you did not ask it to, that is the factory state and not a fault . Press SHIFT + GRID on E to hear it as an ordinary euclidean hat. It ships that way so the switch is audible the moment you plug in. How switching a kind works SHIFT + GRID switches the selected channel between drum and voice behaviour. The engine is never swapped. A drum kit gets the Turing generator, and a synth gets euclid. On a sampler the register walks the kit's own note list rather than ROOT and SCALE, because there a note selects a sample and scale-quantising would land most steps on empty keys — silence with nothing to explain it. On a synth, euclid becomes a root pulse : ROOT plus that channel's OCTAVE, on every hit. Each channel keeps a separate set of parameters per kind, so switching back and forth does not cost you your settings. Pattern length and division deliberately do not move: they are pattern time, not kind, and the groove must not jump under a switch. The surface says when a channel is not itself. The page indicator reads VOX or DRM , and GRID blinks for as long as the selected channel is on an overridden kind. Switching back clears the override rather than pinning the channel to a kind it merely happens to have today — so a later snapshot putting a different engine on that chain is not overruled by a stale choice nobody remembers making. What it refuses, and why A switch rewrites the pattern , so on a channel you have recorded onto it hands the pattern back to the generator and your take is gone. Hand-edited steps do not survive either, for the same reason turning HITS does not — switching rewrites the line from the generator. A voice switched to drum may arrive silent , because its HITS can read back as 0. The tab draws dashed to say so. That is not a defect: turn HITS up. A defect that was published here has been withdrawn. The buttons beside the big encoder were reported to step a preset once and then stick. They never did: they step every press. What stuck was the name . The value was drawn in a font that fits four characters, and preset banks are full of neighbours that agree on their first four — a padthv1 bank of 67 patches has six called Dusk , Dusk2 … Dusk6 , and stepping walks a bank alphabetically. Six presses, one word on the screen, six variants of one pad. Names now draw in the small font at nine characters and keep their trailing digits , so every press shows its move. Fifty starting points The rig ships with fifty more snapshots beside the factory one , numbered 031 to 080 in bank 000 . Ten each of house, deep house, minimal, dub and trance, from 118 to 140 BPM, across 21 synth engines and 24 drum machines. They are fixed arrangements, not generative patches. Every voice arrives at LOCK — MELODY and RHYTHM both 0 — and nothing is modulated. Load one and it plays the same bar until you change something. That is deliberate: the rest of this instrument is about evolution, and these are the places to start from. Turn MELODY up and the preset becomes generative under your hands. The five drum channels keep their roles. A is always the kick and E always the open hat; what changes is the machine — TR909 for house, TR808 and CR78 for dub, TR606 for minimal, SP-1200 for lo-fi. Kits are mixed across channels the way they are on a record, so a 909 kick can sit under an 808 clap. 031 – 060 use the delay and reverb you already know. 061 – 080 replace that pair with something else on every chain — tape and chorus, vinyl and room, phaser and hall — a different pair on each, none repeated. On those twenty, the REVERB and DELAY encoders still send to whatever now occupies those two slots, so the labels stay put while the sound does not. Load one from the touchscreen, inside bank 000 . Nothing is created or destroyed while you play, so a snapshot change is the one moment the audio graph is rebuilt. See also Deep parameter control — reaching everything else a plugin publishes Generating patterns — the two generators a channel can run Mixing and effects — LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY across the row

title: The surface
body: The surface What every button does, how to read the two displays, and the list to work down when a channel goes quiet. Modes and pages Five buttons latch a mode, and exactly one is lit at any time. Button on the panel Mode The eight encoders become CONTROL CONTROL what the selected channel sounds like STEP STEP what the selected channel plays ALL ALL the machine's globals VOLUME MIXER one level across all eight channels AUTO FILTER one filter control across all eight channels A mode can carry more than one page. The arrows beside the display step through that mode's ring and wrap; the page name sits in the middle of the display. Each mode remembers its own page separately for drum and voice channels, so changing channel does not throw you onto a page you were not on. Pressing the mode you are already in returns you to page 1 of that mode. It does not switch you anywhere — every mode button means the same thing twice over: this mode, from the top . Group A–H selects the channel. Pads, tabs and all eight encoders follow immediately, and the inverted tab on the display — never a Group LED — is the authority on which channel is selected. Reading the displays Both displays carry a tab row across the top — A–D on the left, E–H on the right — with four encoder columns under each. The inverted tab is the selected channel. A dashed tab means that channel is not sounding , whether it is muted at the mixer or silenced by its own generator. It is the one mechanism this instrument has for explaining silence, so read the tab row before assuming a fault. A KICK B SNAR C CLAP D CHAT KIT SP12 SAMPLE 0003 cutoff ---- reso ---- A drum channel on CONTROL. CUTOFF and RESO draw dead in lower case with ---- : a sampler has no filter to reach, and the encoder does nothing rather than pretending. What the lights mean Surface What it says Group A–H hue is the channel, brightness is its level, dark means it is not sounding Mode buttons exactly one lit, always — it cannot disagree with the display F1–F8 lit while that channel is muted PLAY lit while anything is running REC lit only when a take is actually possible — dark in STEP mode and while MOD is active GRID lit always, and blinking while the selected channel is on an overridden kind NOTE REPEAT lit only while the selected channel behaves as a voice SWING lit while MOD is held or latched TEMPO lit while it is held, and only then — it does not latch Arrows, ERASE, SHIFT lit whenever the instrument is running — they always do the same thing The buttons, one by one NOTE REPEAT — the register undo. On a voice, it gives back the previous Turing line: it restores the earlier registers — both of them, so the rhythm cannot move out from under a line you just recovered — forces MELODY and RHYTHM to 0 so it holds, and rewrites immediately. It walks back up to four registers, which is roughly two wraps of human reaction time — the window in which a mutation steals a phrase before your hand arrives. It does nothing on a euclidean channel, which is why it is unlit there. DUPLICATE does nothing. The register undo used to live here and moved to NOTE REPEAT, beside the big encoder with the other master controls. TEMPO — hold it and every encoder turns twice as fast. The knobs are deliberately fine, so that a value can be crept up on rather than jumped over. TEMPO is how you cross a range in a hurry: hold it to get near, let go to land. It changes nothing but speed, it does not latch, and it does not set the tempo — that lives on the touchscreen. SHIFT + GRID switches the selected channel's kind — see Sound and presets . A bare GRID press does nothing, deliberately. MOD + ERASE + ALL clears every modulator at once, returning each value to the base you set — see Modulation . The two buttons beside the big encoder step the selected channel's sound, and which sound depends on the engine: previous or next sample on a drum engine, previous or next preset on a synth engine. Hold SHIFT and they step the kit instead , on a drum engine only. Mute, solo and erase F1–F8 mute channels A–H , regardless of which channel is selected — F3 always mutes CLAP. Tap and it latches; hold past a quarter of a second and it is momentary, back on release. Same button, both gestures: momentary is how you play a gesture, latched is how you make a decision. The mute is on the mixer strip rather than the sequencer track , which is why it survives a snapshot, shows on the touchscreen mixer, and takes the channel's reverb and delay tail with it. SOLO works the same two ways. ERASE + a Group button silences that channel — or, on a channel you have recorded onto, hands the pattern back to the generator. Transport Play starts or stops all eight channels together. The decision is taken once and applied to all eight, so they cannot drift into opposite states. Restart jumps every playhead to step 0 without stopping — for pulling channels back onto the one after a length change has phased them apart. Press Play once after loading a snapshot: loop mode is re-asserted on every transport start, and a fresh load is the one moment it may need it. When it goes quiet Work down this list before suspecting the rig. Most of it is things you did. Check What it looks like Is the tab dashed? the channel is muted, or its generator is silent HITS on a drum 0 hits is a silent channel, not a broken one CHANCE at 0 on a drum, no steps left on a voice nothing fires Is something soloed? every non-soloed Group button goes dark MASTER on the ALL page the global level, easy to leave down GATE at its floor on a voice a slow-attack patch never gets far enough to sound A voice that is locked is not silent — LOCK freezes the pattern, it does not mute it. If a whole channel is dead while its tab looks healthy, the fault is below the instrument: see Internals for how the chain is wired, and Manual installation for the checks that catch a stale MIDI route. See also Generating patterns — what HITS, CHANCE, MELODY and RHYTHM actually do Playing and recording — the pad colours in full Modulation — what the ~ and the dashed bar mean
